source: That branch of the lake of Como which extends southwards between two unbroken chains of mountains, and is all bays and gulfs as the mountains advance and recede, narrows down at one point into the form of a river, between a promontory on one side and a wide shore on the other; and the bridge which here links the two banks seems to emphasize this transformation, and to mark the point at which the lake ends and the Adda begins, only to become a lake once more where the banks draw farther apart again, letting the water broaden out and expand into new gulfs and bays. The country bordering the lake, formed by the deposits of three great torrents, is backed by two neighbouring mountains, one called San Martino, and the other, in the Lombard dialect, the Resegone, from its saw-like row of peaks; so that on first seeing it — so long as it is in profile — looking northwards, for instance, from the ramparts of Milan — one can pick it out at once, on the name alone, from the vast and lengthy range of other mountains of obscurer name and more ordinary form. For a considerable stretch the country rises slowly and continuously; then it breaks up into little hills and valleys and into steep and level tracts, following the structure of the two mountains and the erosion of the water. The shore itself, intersected by the beds of torrents, is almost entirely gravel and pebbles; the rest is fields and vineyards, and scattered towns, villages and farms, with here and there a wood extending right on up the mountain-side. Lecco, which is the largest of these towns and gives its name to the district, lies on the lakeside not far from the bridge, and is even apt to find itself partly in the lake when this is high; it is a big town nowadays, well on the way to becoming a city. At the time of the events which we are about to describe, this township which was already of some importance, was also fortified, and so had the honour of housing a commandant and the advantage of a permanent garrison of Spanish soldiers, who taught modesty to the wives and daughters of the town, tickled up the shoulders of an occasional husband and father, and, towards the end of summer, never failed to scatter themselves among the vineyards, to thin out the grapes and lighten the labours of the vintage for the peasants. Paths and tracks used to run — and still do — from one to another of these villages, from the mountain heights to the lakeside, and from one precipice to the other. Sometimes they run steep, sometimes level, and often drop suddenly and bury themselves between two walls, from which, when one looks up, only a patch of sky and some mountain peak can be discerned. Sometimes they come out on open terraces; thence the eye ranges over prospects of varying extent, always full of interest and always changing, as each point of vantage takes in different aspects of the vast landscape, and as one part or the other is foreshortened, or stands out, or disappears. One can see a piece here, another there, and then again a long stretch of that great varied mirror of the water; on this side the lake is shut in at one end, or rather lost among the ins and outs and groupings of the mountains, then spreads out again between more mountains, unfolding one by one, and reflected upside down in the water with the villages on the shores; on the other side is more river, then lake, then river again, losing itself in a shining coil among the mountains, which follow it, getting smaller and smaller until they too are almost lost in the horizon. The very spot from which so many different views can be seen itself appears in views from every side. The mountain on whose foothills you are walking unfolds its cliffs and pinnacles above and around you, each standing out on its own and changing at every step, turning what had just seemed a single ridge into a whole series of ridges, and showing on a height something that a moment before had seemed down on the shore; the quiet and cosy character of these foothills pleasantly tempers the wildness around, and is a foil for the grandeur of the rest of the landscape.

rows.text:
The channel that divides Africa from Europe narrows here to a shallow trough of water, and the seabed rises beneath it like a shoulder pushing up through cloth, so that a stone island surfaces where no island should be, closer to the Tunisian shelf than to the peninsula that administers it; and because the shelf is Africa's while the register is Europe's, the rock has been asked to hold two geographies at once, and it holds them badly, and around it the shipping lanes bend to avoid the shoals that the charts mark in a hatching no mariner reads without wanting to be elsewhere, though the ferries come anyway, and the patrol hulls come, and the water, which cannot be asked anything, goes on lifting and letting fall whatever floats.

Along the northern flank the limestone stands up in cliffs the wind has undercut, and the swell works below in the caves it has been widening for ten thousand years; the coastline that results is a sequence of shallow bays and blind inlets, each holding its own colour of light, each ending in a beach too small to be named on the maps the coast guard uses. The stone leans out above the water. The water goes on eating the stone.

Southward the land slopes down toward a harbour that shelters an unequal fleet: the wooden boats, which arrive; the grey boats, which meet them; the tenders of an agency whose acronym is stencilled on their flanks in a blue that the salt is already lifting.

On the mole a container office has been fitted with a generator and a mast, and inside it a screen shows the sea as a field of returns, each return a tremor that an operator must decide either to name a vessel or to dismiss as chop, since the radar cannot be taught to see intention.

Above the harbour, on the ridge the fishermen call the Spine, three white radomes sit in a row like eggs left by something enormous, and cables run from them down through the prickly pear to a compound whose fence the wind has silvered, and the compound has a gate, and the gate has a logbook, and the logbook is the only place where the sea's traffic becomes countable, because a hull that has crossed the median line without appearing in that book has, so far as the file is concerned, not crossed anything at all.

Twice a week an aircraft leaves the strip to fly the box assigned to it, and the box is a rectangle drawn on nothing.

Nothing marks the line beneath it: no buoy, no change of colour, no shift in the temper of the swell; the water contracts to a defined width only in the ledger, and the ledger is ashore.

A boat that ceases, at that unmarked instant, to be a matter for Tunis becomes a matter for Rome, and the name of what it carries changes with it, and no one aboard feels the change, and the only witness is a satellite fix logged in a column at a desk in a room with the blinds down.

Off the eastern point the sea does what it does everywhere and here in particular: it opens, spreading out to the horizon in a dilation so wide that the eye gives up on it and turns back; then it narrows into the throat between the point and the little island, where it hardens, thickens, compresses itself into a race that pulls at the moorings; and beyond the throat it opens again, unclenching into the long swell of the open channel, which is where the crossings begin and where, in the phrase the reports prefer, assistance is rendered.

The gulls stand on the breakwater in a line the wind arranges for them each morning.

In the flat calm before dawn the searchlight on the cutter falls on the cliff and is thrown back inverted from the water beneath it, so that the rock is seen once standing and once hanging, and the mirror that performs the inversion is only the harbour surface, unbroken; and in these years, as the arrivals rise and the budgets rise with them, that doubled cliff is photographed nightly by cameras nobody has ever needed to explain, and taught to whoever arrives that the rock is generous, and instructed in what shelter means.

The channel that divides two continents narrows here, between the shoal of Africa and the last splintered outcrops of Europe, and where the seafloor rises the water changes its colour, so that a pilot looking down from the low cloud can read the island before he sees it, a pale table of limestone set in indigo, ringed by a shelf of turquoise that seems to hold it up the way a hand holds up a coin; and because the currents that come from the south are warm, and because the wind that comes from the northwest is not, the two bodies meet in a seam of shivering water, a line no chart draws, which the fishermen still know how to find and which the patrol craft have learned to loiter along, waiting.

The sea contracts to a strait and swells again; and along that swelling the cliffs of the island stand up in tiers of chalk and rubble, tiers which the rain has grooved and the salt has candied, tiers on which nothing grows but caper and thyme and a wire fence, so that where the goats once wandered the wind now carries a wire's thin humming. The long low light lies down across the stone. Because the harbour lies to the south, the north coast is left to the swell alone, which has undercut it, hollowing galleries and blowholes that breathe.

The bay opens like a cupped palm below the town; and there the shallows go so clear that a hull seems to float on nothing at all, a slab of shadow suspended, while the sand that lies beneath it holds the ribbed prints which the last easterly pressed there.

A jetty of poured concrete runs out from the quarry road, patched, rust-bled, ending in a bollard; and it is here, where the water is chest-deep and calm, that the launches come alongside to unload, and here that the plastic keels which crossed from the far shore are stacked in the sun to soften, split, and go to powder.

The island's one road climbs from the port and forks, and the western fork ends at the airstrip, whose long grey bar you see plain from the sea, and whose whole length you see again, reversed and trembling, in the film of standing water that lies on the apron after rain; and the eastern fork ends at a gate, and past the gate stands a compound of prefabricated blocks with numbered doors, a fenced yard, a canteen, and a bank of floodlights that come on at dusk and burn until the boats are counted.

The lamps are set to assist the rescue, and the fence is set to protect the rescued, and the register is kept for their instruction.

They are gathered from the water; they are taught the procedure, entered, photographed, and issued a number; and after the number is issued the name goes into a drawer.

Where the shelf drops away the blue turns to ink, and the swell out there gathers weight, and the crests begin to comb over, and a hull the length of a bus becomes, at three miles, a splinter that the eye loses whenever the trough takes it.

At the twelfth mile from the shore a boat is a boat, unnamed and unnumbered, and nothing on it changes; but the log of the coordinated centre closes at that longitude, and another log opens, and the vessel that was a case of distress becomes, in the space of a metre of water no eye can see, an interception, or nothing, or a matter for the other shore; the line does not exist on the sea, which shows a level face; it exists on the transcript, whose column of figures the operator reads aloud, and by that reading the thing is renamed while the sea, indifferent, keeps swelling and subsiding.

The whole coast beats to that rhythm, the rhythm which the passage itself follows out to the horizon.

As I write this the moles are lengthening: a dredger works the inner basin, the cranes come by barge, and the concrete goes down in caissons that will widen the berth, so that the shelf which the reefs and inlets once broke into bays and inlets is being drawn into one straight face of grey, and the swell that met the rock and drew back from it now meets only itself, subsiding and swelling against a wall built to hold.

The channel that divides the two continents narrows here to a bright corridor, and where the last shelf of Africa slides under the water it does not so much end as continue in another key, so that the island standing above it — a low table of limestone lifted clear of the shallows, scoured, treeless, so pale at noon that the light seems to come up out of the rock rather than fall on it — belongs, if one consults the charts, to Europe, though the wind that combs it comes off the desert, and the swell that works its southern cliffs has crossed nothing but Libyan water to arrive, and the birds that stop in its gardens are only pausing, having elected to break a longer flight, meaning to leave again before the harbour lamps come on.

The coast bends and slackens along that southern flank in a rhythm the eye learns quickly: coves that hold no sand, ledges the sea has undercut until they hang, a single beach of white shell where the turtles come ashore to bury what they carry. The cliffs stand up in slow deliberate tiers of stone; the water beneath them dilates and draws in. Northward the shore hardens, and the cliff runs unbroken for two miles, giving nothing back to the swimmer, offering no stair.

Then the land relents into the one deep notch that made the place matter, and the harbour opens: a flooded valley whose mouth faces east, whose floor shelves so gently that a hull may ground far out.

Here the sea, having spread itself all morning over forty miles of open blue, contracts into the throat of the basin, tightening between the mole and the fuel jetty; and this is where the ships assemble, grey and white and grey, riding at moorings that are numbered on a board ashore.

The largest of them, whose flank carries a legend in three languages and whose rails are dressed with orange floats, sits so still that the crane-arm above her is doubled in the oiled water, doubled and reversed, the mirror of the harbour showing her mast driven downward into the mud; and the smaller cutters, which run out at dusk and come in with the light, lie inboard of her, taking on water, taking on the day's bread, their radar turning even at rest.

The apparatus keeps a school and an office and a gate; the school is a hall where lessons in identity are given, and the gate is counted.

Boats are brought in under escort here, the crews relieved of their engines, and each arrival is received into care, entered, numbered, photographed, and lodged behind a fence whose gauge is fine enough to hold a hand.

The rescue is charitable, the register is pedagogical, and the fingerprint is taken gently, because the machine reads better when the finger has been oiled first; and afterward the ferry goes north at eight, and the aircraft goes north at ten, and the island resumes its size.

Between the outer light and the open water there runs a line that nothing marks — no reef, no change of colour, no shift in the set of the current — and yet a vessel crossing it stops being a vessel in distress and becomes a vessel intercepted, the status altering at the instant a coordinate is logged; the line is invisible in the sea and perfectly visible on the plotter, where it is drawn in red, and it is the plotter that decides, so that men who have been swimming in one jurisdiction climb, dripping, into another, and the water they came out of has no memory of the change.

The whole coast, seen from the ridge, is a sequence of swelling and subsiding, headland and cove, cove and headland.

In this decade the corridor is shifting westward, and the sea widens again beyond the last buoy, dilating toward the Tunisian bank, so that what the charts still call a channel is becoming a field of open crossings; and the undulation that the shoreline makes, subsiding and swelling in bays and inlets, is the same undulation the routes make offshore, and the same one the years will make, drawing in and letting out, drawing in and letting out again.

The channel that divides two continents narrows here, between the low limestone spine of the island and the invisible line drawn on the charts of three ministries, and it narrows so far that the water, which has come broadening out of the Gulf of Sirte and has spread itself across four hundred miles of open swell without meeting anything that might oblige it to choose a direction, is compelled at last to gather, to thin, to run in a single grey artery past the harbour mouth; and where the current tightens, the coastguard patrol keeps station, so that its wake may instruct the smaller boats and its floodlight may offer guidance to whoever has lost the shore.

The cliffs stand up sheer above that traffic, ochre where the sun has bleached them and rust-dark in the fissures that hold water after rain, and because the strata lie almost level the whole southern face reads like a ledger left open on a table. Below the cliffs the coves begin to pocket the swell. A helicopter drags its shadow up the rock, and the shadow ripples where the rock will not lie flat.

There are two islands here, in effect: the one the ferries know, which has a mole and a fuel line and a customs shed, and the one the charts call a reception point, which has a perimeter, a road that ends, and a gate that opens inward.

The sea between them is not a single thing but a sequence of names, and each name is written somewhere in a filing cabinet in a city four hundred miles north; a hull leaves the territorial band and becomes, without altering its bearing, a matter for a different desk, a different rescue protocol, a different arithmetic of who must go and fetch it.

The strait, having opened out to its full breadth off the African shelf, where the depth soundings run to nine hundred metres and the swell has room to build without breaking, contracts as it approaches the island's western headland, squeezing itself between shoal and shoal until it is scarcely a mile of navigable water, and then it lets go again, and it dilates eastward toward the deep trench, and the pilots, who read the surface as a text, say the water gives itself away there: it is unable to hide the shape of what lies under it.

The lighthouse throws its beam across the shoals to warn the traffic off, and the same beam is thrown back doubled and inverted in the wet basalt of the tide-line.

The floodlights are switched on at dusk; they scour the whole of the anchorage, and they pick out the marker buoys, and they make the water briefly legible, so that nothing may cross unobserved.

Everything in this place is inventoried: the sea comes and goes, the boats come and go, and the buses come and go along the single road, and even the wind, which arrives from the south charged with dust when the season turns, is logged hourly in a register kept above the port.

At this moment, in the years since the crossings multiplied, the island's stone is being turned into a filing system: the field above the airstrip that once held nothing but wild caper is now a compound of numbered containers; the small cemetery, which had room enough for the families who fished here, has been extended twice; and the boats themselves, which are hauled up and stacked behind the fence, are being eaten by salt and by sun until their planking goes the colour of the cliff, and the cliff, which loses a little of itself to every winter storm, takes them back.

Then the swell subsides, and the coves and the bays lie still that had been swelling and subsiding all night.

Look down from the headland at first light and you will see the whole undulation of it — the water moving in long troughs and crests toward the mole, the road climbing and dropping over the limestone, the queue at the gate lengthening and thinning as the officers work — and because the undulation never stops, and because every wave that flattens on the beach is followed by one already forming behind it, the island keeps arriving at itself, which is what it will go on doing.

The channel that runs between the shelf of Africa and the last crumb of Europe narrows here to a corridor of open water, and the corridor is not marked, though everything crossing it is counted, so that a hull leaving Zuwarah at dusk enters a space which has no line drawn on its surface and yet is divided, minute by minute, into sectors that each carry a name in a different registry, and the sectors overlap where the registries disagree, and the disagreement is where the sea is emptiest; and the island itself lies at the corridor's northern lip, low, pale, scoured, a slab of limestone tilted so that its cliffs face the continent it belongs to and its harbours open toward the one it does not, as if to receive what arrives and to keep what arrives from arriving were the same gesture performed twice.

The rock shelves into the water in long tables which the swell has undercut, and beneath them the sand goes white; the light comes up through it so that boats float on a brightness rather than a depth, and swimmers hang in the green as though suspended in air. Above, the patrol shed keeps its aerial turning, a slow bright vane that combs the offing all night for what the offing carries, and the sweep it makes is patient, is unhurried, is exactly as regular as breath. (RE-DERIVED)

Two harbours serve the place, and they serve unequally: the old basin takes trawlers and the ferry from the north, while the new quay, fenced in blue mesh, takes what the cutters bring in at four in the morning, when nobody who is not paid to be awake is awake.

The cutters themselves are grey, low, and very clean, vessels whose names commemorate virtues; they carry gantries and davits and, amidships, a folded orange ladder that goes down the side to the waterline where the transfer happens.

From the quay a road climbs between prickly pear and cinderblock to the compound on the ridge, and the compound has two gates, one of which is used to admit and the other of which is never seen to open; a wind fence of green plastic runs the length of the wire, meant to break the gusts, meant also to break the sightline, so that the yard inside can be heard and not read.

Beyond the compound the ground falls away again to the southern coves, and there the water performs its two natures: it widens, it slackens, it lies out across the whole plate of the horizon in a single unbroken sheet which no headland interrupts, and then, drawing in toward the throat of a cove whose walls stand nine metres apart, it gathers, it tightens, it compresses itself into a green muscle that shoves and sucks in the rock's cavities; and past the cove mouth, released, it spreads once more, dilating outward until the eye can no longer find where the spreading stops.

The channel, seen from the ridge, shows two things at once: the actual traffic upon it, and the same traffic inverted in the wet slate of the flats below, where masts hang downward.

The eye reads the mast, the water repeats the mast upside down, the radar screen in the shed writes it a third time as a fleck; and the fleck is what the log records, because the log is the only one of the three that keeps.

A vessel crossing this water changes its name without changing anything else, for at a coordinate that the water does not mark it ceases to be a case of rescue and becomes a case of interception, and it ceases to be a case of interception and becomes a case of transfer, and the boundary is legible only in the ledger.

Southward the coves take the swell in slow sets, each set rising, each set breaking, the interval between them long enough that a listener counts it; and on calmer mornings, when the surface goes flat as poured glass, the sets stop altogether and the water only leans, and its leaning, which is not a wave and not a stillness, moves along the whole southern shore from the light to the point in one continuous flexure, so that the coast seems to be answering something a long way off, something that has not yet arrived but is coming, a listing motion the island has been reading for thirty years and reads again this season.

Under the leaning water, at nine metres, lie the hulls that were lifted out of the traffic and sunk here.

In these last few winters the shoreline is losing its dune at the rate of a metre a year, and the wire above the beach, which was set back when the fence went up, now stands where the sand was; the sea takes what it likes, and the compound teaches those it holds the words for its own procedures, and the cutters go out at three, and go out again at four, and bring in, each dawn, whatever the corridor has released to them, and the aerial turns, and the light on the point turns, and the ledger fills.

The channel that divides the two great basins narrows here between a shelf of African rock and the drowned shoulder of Sicily, and the water, having gathered its whole southward weight above the sill, thins as it passes, so that where the seabed rises to meet it the current quickens and combs itself into ridges, and the ridges break, and the broken water spreads again to seaward, dilating into that pale blue plain which the charts are content to leave unnamed; and because the island stands athwart the narrowing, it takes the swell first on its southern cliffs, where the limestone has been hollowed to receive it, and lets the rest run past to widen and to slacken and to forget, in the greater openness beyond, that it was ever pressed.

The island itself is a raft of tilted stone, low at the north where the cliffs stand up to the weather and lower at the south where the coves lie open, and its whole surface, which grows nothing taller than a caper bush, slopes so gently to the water that a walker who leaves the airstrip at first light will not know he has begun to descend until the salt is on his mouth. The stone lies bare and dry. The wind combs down the terraces.

There is one harbour, cut into the eastern flank, whose two moles reach toward each other and do not meet; and inside that gap, which measures perhaps eighty metres, the sea keeps a stillness that the sea outside has never learned.

Beyond the moles the swell recovers itself, and there the water begins again to widen, to lift, to run in long unhurried lines that seem to travel without effort, though anyone who has watched them arrive from a hull knows the effort is entirely theirs; and the lines that pass the harbour mouth are the same lines that will find the beaches to the west.

Above the harbour, on the ridge that the road climbs, stands a compound of white containers, which the register calls a centre of first reception, and which receives, at hours the sea determines and not the road, those whom the sea has delivered; and within it the apparatus that the continent maintains here undertakes to instruct the newly landed in the procedures that concern them, to relieve them of the numbers they carried, and to assign them numbers of its own, so that each person who enters the gate as a name leaves the gate as an entry, and the entry travels north while the person waits.

The officers speak of teaching the sea's arrivals the geography of their rights, and of caring for them in the fenced yard until a vessel is available.

At the same hour the grey cutters put out from the mole, and they go quickly, and they go far, for the line they are sent to hold is not drawn on the water; and the water carries no line at all.

What the cutter does when it reaches that unmarked place is turn, and wait, and take aboard, and hand across to a hull flying another flag, and the handing is entered in a log; and the log, being a document, decides what has happened.

For the same wooden boat, riding the same swell with the same load, is a vessel in distress at one longitude and an irregular departure at another, and the boundary between the two conditions has no colour, no reef, no change of temperature: the rescue ceases and the interception commences at a point which exists only in the coordinates that a screen in a room on the ridge writes down, and the boat, which knows nothing of screens, feels the water beneath it neither tighten nor loosen as it crosses.

From the cliff at the southern point one sees the low sun on the water, and sees it again inverted in the wet lens of a patrol boat's windscreen.

Now, in these years of increasing traffic, the beaches to the west receive what the current brings: a plank, a sandal, a jerrican rinsed white; and the sea, which had narrowed at the sill and pressed itself through, is opening once more beyond the island into that vast slackened brightness where nothing is held, so that a visitor standing there at evening, watching the whole surface swell and subside, subside and swell, will take the movement for peace, because peace is what such motion resembles.

The channel that divides two continents narrows here to a corridor of open water, and the seabed beneath it rises as though it meant to touch the air, and the rise breaks the surface at last in a spine of white limestone no higher than a warehouse roof, which the charts call an island and the Africans call a landing, and which lies so far south of the peninsula that governs it that a bird leaving its cliffs at dawn to feed will reach Tunisia before the customs office opens, while the ferries from Sicily labour all night northward to keep it supplied, and the water on either flank of the corridor deepens again to a blue that seems to withdraw from measurement, so that the island appears less a summit than a checkpoint the sea has agreed to maintain.

The stone lifts from that water in low terraces which no rain has softened, and the wind that comes off the Gulf of Gabès has scoured them until nothing grows on them but caper and thorn; the harbour bites into the southern flank, a bay so sheltered that a hull can rest in it without a rope, and a road climbs from the quay past the fuel drums and the folded tents, and the airstrip lies along the ridge above, and every summer the light comes down so white on that ridge that the runway numbers vanish beneath it.

To the north the coast gives nothing at all: cliff after cliff of chalk falling ninety metres into surge, unbroken, unlanded, and the swell arrives against it from three hundred kilometres of nothing, so that the noise never entirely stops.

The cliffs run east until they collapse into the rubble bay that the guidebooks photograph, whose sand the turtles use, and the water there is the colour of glass held to a lamp; but the currents that gather off the point have carried the drowned to that beach every winter since anyone kept count.

At the western end the land finishes in a rock stack, sheer, split from the cliff by a channel too narrow to row through, and the gulls hold it, and the radar mast on the headland behind it turns, and turns, sweeping a cone of attention out over the corridor to find whatever moves; the mast is painted the same white as the stone, which the engineers say was a courtesy to the landscape.

The mast is not the only eye: from the coastguard station on the height a lens tracks the horizon, and the horizon gives back a shudder of heat that lifts distant hulls off the water and hangs them upside down above their own wakes, an image the officers have learned to distrust; and the thermal camera, which sees no colour, renders the same boats as pale smears on a black field, so that a vessel appears twice in the same minute — once inverted in the air, once reversed in the screen — and it is the second appearance, the one made of instruments, that goes into the log, because the log requires numbers.

The apparatus describes its own work in the language of rescue, and every hull brought under tow is entered as an assistance rendered.

The centre above the harbour is called a hotspot; it teaches new arrivals the procedures of the Union, and it takes their fingerprints for their protection, and it keeps them behind a fence, and the fence is the same green as the pines.

The prints go into a database in Strasbourg, and the database returns a name, and the name determines a corridor, and the corridor ends either at a mainland reception hall or on a chartered flight south, and nobody at the quay says which, since the sorting is held to be an administrative rather than a geographical fact.

South of the island the corridor widens: for thirty kilometres the water opens, and the light spreads across it without interruption, and then the opening tightens again into the strait itself, where two coastguards from two continents patrol lanes that are pressed together within sight of each other, and the sea contracts to a lane, and a lane to a wake; and only past the strait's throat does it dilate once more into the great southern basin, which no patrol reaches, and in which the water is simply water, swelling and subsiding under weather, undisturbed by nomenclature, until a hull enters it and the naming begins.

Because everything that governs the island is drawn in lines, the lines matter more than the stone.

A boat crosses a meridian that has no colour and no surface, and on the far side of it the same boat, the same fuel, the same people cease to be an emigration and recommence as an arrival, and the change is legible nowhere in the water but only in the plotter's trace, in the timestamp, in the entry a duty officer makes; and in these years the corridor is shifting again, the lanes moving eastward as the patrols move, so that the island's stone stays and the border around it subsides and swells like a tide.

The channel narrows here, where the shelf of Africa climbs toward a limestone table that the currents have been shaving for ten thousand years, and the water, having darkened over the deep trench to the north, lightens again as it comes onto the banks, so that anyone standing on the ridge above the harbour can see, laid out beneath him, the two blues divided by a line he cannot cross with his eye; and because the island lies nearer to one continent than to the other, and because the sea keeps no ledgers, the boats come; and the patrol vessels go out to meet them, to instruct the helmsmen in the safer bearings, to relieve the overloaded hulls of their passengers, to teach the crossing its proper limits.

The rock rises hard from the water and lies down flat along its spine, a wafer of pale stone tilted north, and the coves on the southern flank, which the swell enters slowly and leaves more slowly still, hold sand so fine it squeaks; and to the north the cliffs stand sheer above a sea that gives back nothing, no shelf, no landing, and there the gulls that nest in the fissures wheel out over an emptiness their cries do not measure, while the wind, which arrives from the south nine months of the year, presses the low scrub eastward until it grows sideways out of the fractured ground.

Everything on the island leans one way, and the fig trees crouch where the ground gives them cover; the walls of dry stone run seaward in long fingers so that the goats, when the gales come, may find some corner out of the weather.

The harbour cuts into the eastern shore in a hook of deep water, which the fishing fleet shares now with the grey hulls; on its inner mole stand the sheds that were built for nets and are used for other inventories, and the cranes that once lifted only ice.

Below the mole the water is clear to seven metres, and a swimmer looking down can count the anchor chains, the drowned tyres, the ribs of the wooden boats that were towed in and stripped and left to settle, which the authorities have arranged in the shallows to keep them out of the fairway, a graveyard the harbourmaster prefers to call a repository, though nothing there is kept.

Out past the mole the sea widens, and the horizon runs unbroken from the eastern point to the western, and there is nothing in that whole compass except the light on the water and, twice a day, the shadow of an aircraft; but the surface, which shows the sky in reverse, holds the aircraft too, and holds it upside down, so that the watcher on the cliff sees the machine pass above him and sees the same machine slide inverted beneath him along the polished swell, the sea being the only mirror on the island large enough to take it whole.

The radar mast on the high ground turns without pause, and the screen in the room below shows the channel as a grey disc across which the returns crawl and fade and crawl again.

The vessels come in at first light; a cutter noses to the quay, a launch waits, and a bus stands at the head of the ramp with its engine running, since the reception of the arrivals is arranged before the arrivals arrive.

Down the ramp they come, and the count begins, and the wristbands are issued, and the numbers are entered into a register that will follow each body inland, though the register, which has no column for the sea, records only the hour of the landing.

Somewhere out in the channel, invisible, unmarked by any buoy, there runs a line the water does not know: a hull that crosses it eastward is a vessel in distress and must be assisted; the same hull, having crossed it westward, is an illegal conveyance and may be turned back, and the crew of the patrol boat learn which of these two things they are looking at by reading the coordinates off an instrument, since the boundary declares itself nowhere on the surface, in no change of colour, in no shift of the swelling and subsiding water, which goes on doing what it did before the line was drawn.

The sea, having widened all afternoon, contracts toward evening into the narrow lane the searchlights open across it.

In these years the light on the water is joined by other lights, and the channel that the fishermen once read by the subsiding and swelling of its own body is read now by satellites, so that the pilots know where every hull sits while the hulls themselves know nothing, and the island, which is a table of stone eight kilometres long, goes on tilting its one face south toward the water that keeps arriving, in bays and in inlets, patient, wave upon wave, undulating as it has always undulated, toward whatever the next morning brings up onto the sand.

The channel that divides Africa from Europe narrows here without narrowing on any chart, and the water, running north from the shelf where the seabed climbs, is pressed into a corridor between two banks of shoal so that the current, which the fishermen call the throat because it swallows, quickens as it rises, and the island stands in the middle of it like a knuckle of limestone set out to break the swell, and the coast guard cutters, which are stationed at the harbour mouth to protect the crossing, go out at dusk to instruct the small boats in the proper direction, and the surveillance drones circle to keep watch over those who have not asked to be watched, and everything the eye takes in from the ridge is at once a geography and a procedure.

The island lies low and long against the light, a slab of white rock tipped seaward, and its northern flank drops in cliffs that the wind has undercut into shelves and hollows where the gulls nest, while the southern flank slopes into coves whose sand is the colour of bone and whose water shelves so gradually that a hull can ground a hundred metres out; and on the height above the town the radar mast turns, sweeping its slow arc over a sea it has learned to read as traffic.

Below the mast the reception centre stands behind a double fence, and the road to it climbs between prickly pear and rusted rebar; the men and women who arrive walk up it in file, because the buses are seldom running and the distance is not thought to be great.

The harbour, which faces east and shelters everything, holds the fishing fleet along its inner quay and the grey patrol hulls along its outer; between them lies the pontoon where the landings are counted, and the tally is written in a ledger that never leaves the office.

The sea beyond the breakwater seems to widen as the afternoon lengthens, opening and flattening until it appears to have no edge at all, and only from the lighthouse can a watcher learn to see where the shelf falls away, where the blue tightens to indigo and closes; the fishermen say the water there begins to hold, and they prefer not to be caught in it after dark.

Twelve nautical miles out, at the line that no eye can find, the water that was territorial becomes international, and a hull that was a rescue obligation becomes a matter for negotiation, and the change is registered nowhere in the swell itself but only in the transponder, which logs the crossing to the second, and in the plotter that draws the boundary as a thin dotted seam across a surface that carries no seam, so that the same wave which broke against a jurisdiction a moment ago breaks now against a protocol.

The cliffs stand in the water and hang inverted in it, doubled by that oiled and glassy calm which the summer brings, and each ledge repeats itself downward, reversed.

At the foot of one such ledge the wrecks are stacked ashore, painted hulls bleaching, and the paint flakes, and the wood grows light as pumice, and a signboard names the place a memorial, though the boats were brought here to be got out of the way.

The wind shifts after midnight and the sea contracts again, drawing in on itself, narrowing between the shoals, and the swell shortens, and the crossing that looked possible at noon closes like a hand, and the radio traffic thickens, because someone somewhere has already put out from a beach three hundred kilometres south.

By first light the water has slackened and opened once more, dilating to the horizon, and the cutters come in with their decks full; the ledger opens; the count begins. Along the quay the thermal blankets catch the sun, and the volunteers move down the line with water and with forms, and the forms take longer than the water, and a young officer, whose Italian the arrivals cannot follow and whose gestures they can, explains with great patience that they are being helped, that the fingerprinting is for their own protection, that the bus will come.

At this hour of the present decade the fences are being extended eastward, one panel at a time, along ground that was until recently pasture.

The undulation that the eye follows out there — the long lift and settle of the water between the two banks of shoal, the swell that gathers and lets go and gathers — is the island's one constant, and it is the shape of everything that will happen on this rock, since the sea contracts and dilates and contracts, and the crossings likewise come in pulses, thickening in the calm and dying in the gale; and the ledger, which records only arrivals, cannot record the rhythm that produces them.

The channel that divides the two shelves of shallow water narrows here to a strait of some ninety miles, and the seabed, rising as it goes, begins to lift the swell into ridges, so that a vessel crossing must climb and fall, climb and fall, while the current, which sets eastward for most of the year, gathers whatever floats and delivers it toward the island as though it meant to bring each drifting thing safely home, and the reefs, whose ledges are charted in fathoms on papers no one aboard has ever held, teach the hulls what the pilots did not, and the wind, when it comes from the south, arrives already carrying dust.

Then the island lifts out of the water, low and pale and tilted, its northern cliffs turned to the weather like a shoulder, its southern shore let down in coves that shelve so gently a child could walk out fifty yards; and the limestone, which holds no rivers, keeps what rain it takes in cisterns, so that every green thing here is a thing that has bargained; the prickly pear stands in rows along the walls, and the wind combs the low scrub flat, and the light comes off the rock so white at noon that the eye must look down to rest.

The harbor bites into the eastern flank, a long throat of water where the fishing boats lie doubled in their own reflections; the quay smells of diesel and salt, and the stone is worn smooth where ropes have crossed it for a century.

Beyond the mole there is a second basin, dredged and floodlit, in which the gray hulls berth that carry the flags of the agency; a chain-link fence, whose posts are set in fresh concrete, follows the water's edge and turns inland at the fuel tanks.

From the ridge above, the whole apparatus is legible at once: the mast that listens, the low sheds where lists are made, the gate that opens twice a day to let the buses through; and the road, which was cut for lorries and never widened, climbs past the cemetery and drops again toward the interior, where the hangars stand behind their wire, waiting to be filled.

The sea itself is a thing of two tempers, and it changes them without warning: it broadens, it spreads, it opens westward into a plain of hammered light that seems to have no farther shore; then it draws in, it tightens between the headlands, it clenches in the narrow gut below the cliff where the water goes green and sucks; and then, past the last rock, it widens once more, unclenching, dilating, running out to the horizon in bands of blue that carry no mark of anything that has crossed them.

In the flat calm of early morning the cliff stands upright above the water and stands inverted beneath it, doubled in the mirror the sea has become, and every fissure repeats itself downward.

The patrol boat, too, goes doubled: the hull above and the hull below, joined at the waterline, and when the wake reaches the reflection it breaks it into rungs, so that the image climbs and comes apart while the vessel itself holds its course.

The undulation is everywhere here, and it is not only in the water: it is in the ridges of the seabed, and in the terraces cut into the hillside, and in the queues that lengthen and shorten at the gate as each boat is emptied, though nobody standing in them can see where the line begins.

Twelve miles out, the water has one name; inside that line it has another, and the change is written nowhere on the surface, which lies unmarked and identical on both sides of it; only the plotter on the bridge knows, and the plotter says so in a small green figure, and at that figure the jurisdiction of one authority ceases and the jurisdiction of another recommences, and the boat that was a matter for no one becomes, in the space of a single wave, a matter for the officer on watch, who logs the hour and reduces a hundred and eighty people to a number that will be forwarded before dawn.

The register, which is kept in a bound book, is the only place where the boundary is visible.

These past few winters the crossings have been shifting westward, and the wrecks come ashore now on beaches that had none before; the currents that once gathered everything toward the eastern coves gather it now toward the western, and what the sea carries in it delivers with the same indifference to the volunteers who assist the arrivals and to the officers who correct the courses of departing hulls, so that the coves and the bays, the bays and the coves, go on receiving what the strait has lifted and let fall.
